posts.title: The operations guide to accepting stablecoins
posts.excerpt: Settlement timing, reconciliation, refunds, fraud and custody: the operational decisions that determine whether crypto acceptance actually works.
posts.metaDescription: A long-form operational guide for merchants accepting stablecoin payments, covering settlement, reconciliation, refunds, fraud, custody and running a useful pilot.
posts.author: Abisoye Falabi
posts.imageAlt: Hands typing on a laptop at a sunlit desk

toc.label: Why settlement speed changes the business, not just the ledger
What actually happens when a customer pays
Handling refunds without losing money on volatility
Custody, and the question you should ask your provider
Regulatory posture without a legal department
Running a pilot that tells you something

children.text: Accepting stablecoin payments is less a technology decision than an operations one. The integration is the easy part; what determines whether it works is settlement timing, reconciliation, refund policy, and whether your team knows what to do when a customer insists they have paid. This is a working guide to the parts that matter.
Why settlement speed changes the business, not just the ledger

Most merchants think about payments as a cost line: a percentage taken off the top, a fee schedule to negotiate down once a year. That framing hides the part that actually constrains a growing business, which is time. Money that has been authorised but not settled cannot buy inventory, cannot pay a supplier, and cannot fund a marketing push in the week it would have mattered.

Card rails typically settle in one to three business days, and cross-border flows can stretch to five or more once correspondent banks are involved. For a business with thin working capital, that delay is the difference between reordering a bestseller now and reordering it after the moment has passed. Stablecoin settlement collapses that window to minutes, which is a working-capital change rather than a fee change.

The practical effect is that a merchant can run leaner. Less cash parked to cover the settlement gap means more cash deployed into stock, staff, or acquisition. That is the argument worth making internally, and it lands better with a finance lead than a decimal point on interchange.
What actually happens when a customer pays

A crypto checkout looks simple from the outside: the customer picks a wallet, approves a transfer, and the order confirms. Underneath, three things have to line up. The payment has to be constructed for the right chain and token, the transaction has to be observed on that chain, and the merchant has to be credited only once the transaction is final rather than merely broadcast.

The gap between broadcast and final is where most naive integrations go wrong. A transaction visible in the mempool has not happened yet. It can be dropped, replaced by a higher-fee transaction from the same sender, or reorganised out of the chain entirely. Releasing goods on a mempool sighting is functionally the same as shipping against a cheque that has not cleared.

A payment processor earns its place by absorbing that complexity: watching the chain, applying a confirmation policy appropriate to the amount and the network, and only then telling the merchant the money is theirs.
Choosing which chains to accept

Supporting every chain sounds customer-friendly and is usually a mistake. Each additional network adds an integration surface, a set of failure modes, and a liquidity position to manage. The better question is which chains your customers already hold balances on.

In practice a small set covers most volume: an Ethereum layer-two for customers who live in that ecosystem, a low-fee chain for smaller payments where gas would otherwise dominate, and whichever network your treasury already uses for payouts. Start there, watch what customers ask for, and add deliberately.
Fees matter more than they appear. A five dollar payment on a network with three dollar gas is not a payment, it is a donation to validators. Match the network to the basket size.
Handling refunds without losing money on volatility

Refunds are where crypto payments stop resembling card payments. There is no chargeback mechanism and no acquirer to reverse a transaction. A refund is a fresh payment from you to the customer, which means you decide the amount, the token, and the moment.

If you accepted a stablecoin and refund the same stablecoin, the problem is small. If you accepted a volatile asset and refund it days later, you may return more or less value than you received. The usual answer is to denominate the order in fiat, settle in stablecoin, and refund the fiat-equivalent amount in stablecoin, so neither party carries the price risk of the gap.
Write the policy down before the first refund rather than during it. Customers accept a clear rule and resent an improvised one.
Reconciliation and the finance team

The fastest way to lose internal support for a payment method is to make month-end harder. Finance needs every settled payment to map to an order, a fiat value at the time of settlement, and a fee, in a format their existing tooling can ingest.

That means exporting more than a transaction hash. A usable record carries the order reference, the gross amount in the settlement token, the fiat equivalent at settlement time, the network fee, the processor fee, and the timestamp. Anything less and someone is reconciling by hand against a block explorer, which does not scale past a few dozen orders.
Agree the export format with finance during the pilot, not after it.
Fraud looks different here
Card fraud is dominated by stolen credentials and chargeback abuse. Neither applies directly to crypto payments, which removes a familiar category of loss and introduces less familiar ones.

The common attacks are social rather than cryptographic. Falsified payment confirmations, screenshots of transactions that were never broadcast, and pressure to release goods before confirmation. Staff need one rule that is easy to follow under pressure: the dashboard is the source of truth, not the customer.

The second category is address substitution, where an attacker manipulates the payment address a customer sees. Anything that renders a payment address deserves the same scrutiny as code that touches credentials.
Getting the checkout experience right
A crypto checkout that assumes fluency will convert badly. Many customers have used a wallet a handful of times and do not know what a network is, let alone which one they are on.

The details that move conversion are unglamorous: showing the fiat amount prominently and the token amount secondarily, naming the network in plain language, and stating clearly how long confirmation will take before the customer commits. A progress state that says what is happening beats a spinner every time.
Offer crypto alongside existing methods rather than in place of them. The goal is to capture demand that would otherwise leave, not to relitigate how the majority of customers already prefer to pay.
Custody, and the question you should ask your provider

Custody is the single most consequential decision in the stack. A custodial provider holds your funds between settlement and payout, which is convenient and concentrates risk. A non-custodial provider routes funds to addresses you control, which shifts key management onto you.
Neither is universally right. The question worth asking any provider is direct: at what points do you hold my funds, and for how long? An answer that takes several paragraphs is itself informative.

Whichever model you choose, the key-handling practices matter more than the marketing. Private keys should never be shared internally, backups should be tested rather than assumed, and access should be revocable when someone leaves.
Regulatory posture without a legal department

Accepting crypto does not automatically make a business a money services business, but the boundary varies by jurisdiction and by exactly what the business does with the assets afterwards. Converting on behalf of customers, holding balances for third parties, or facilitating transfers between users all move a business closer to a licensable activity.

The pragmatic path for a merchant is to accept payment for its own goods and services, settle promptly into its own accounts, and avoid becoming an intermediary for anyone else. That is a materially different posture from operating an exchange.
Keep records. Sanctions screening and record-keeping obligations are far easier to satisfy continuously than to reconstruct after a question arrives.
Running a pilot that tells you something

A pilot that reaches a handful of orders will not answer whether crypto payments help. Pick a segment where the case is strongest — cross-border customers, higher basket sizes, or a region where card acceptance rates are poor — and run long enough to see repeat behaviour.

Measure three things: incremental orders that would not otherwise have converted, the total cost per order including network fees, and the operational load in hours. The third is the one teams forget, and it is what decides whether the method survives past the pilot.

If the numbers work, expand by segment rather than switching everything at once. If they do not, you will know precisely which of the three failed, which is a far more useful outcome than a vague sense that it did not catch on.
In short:

treat crypto acceptance as a payment method with its own operational shape, not as a card rail with different plumbing. The businesses that get value from it are the ones that changed a process, not just a checkout.

posts.title: How to Stay Safe with Crypto: A Simple Guide for Merchants
posts.excerpt: Crypto payments cannot be reversed, so the scams matter. Here are the ones merchants run into most, and the habits that keep your wallet secure.
posts.metaDescription: Common crypto scams merchants run into, and the security practices that keep your wallet, your business, and your customers safe.
posts.author: Abisoye Falabi
posts.imageAlt: Hands typing on a laptop at a sunlit desk

toc.label: Best Practices for Securing Your Cryptocurrency

children.text: As a merchant, accepting cryptocurrency opens your business to customers across borders and allows fast, secure payments. However, crypto transactions are permanent. This means that if your crypto assets are stolen or sent to the wrong wallet address, they cannot be reversed. That’s why securing your crypto assets is important for protecting both your business and your customers’ trust.

In this guide, we have highlighted some of the common scams out there and have provided best safety practices to help you keep your crypto assets safe without running into the hands of bad actors or scammers.
Common scam methods
Phishing emails:

Scammers usually send emails pretending to be from your wallet provider or exchange, urging you to click a link to “verify” your account. The link leads to a fake site that steals your login details. As a Stablezact merchant you should always type the official website address directly into your browser instead of clicking links in messages.
Imitation platforms:

Fraudulent websites or apps are designed to look identical to real exchanges so you will trust them with your credentials. Only download apps from official app stores and bookmark the correct site so you never risk clicking on a counterfeit one.
Social media impersonation:

Fake accounts pose as influencers, business partners, or even customer support agents, sending private messages with offers or urgent requests. Always confirm identities through a separate, trusted communication channel before responding.
Fake customer payment confirmations:

Scammers send altered screenshots showing proof of payment to get merchants to release goods before the crypto actually arrive in your wallet. Always check your Stablezact merchant dashboard to confirm a transaction before delivering goods or services. You can also double check transactions on blockchain explorers like Etherscan, Bscscan etc.
Best Practices for Securing Your Cryptocurrency
Never share your private key:

Your private wallet is like the key to your business vault. Anyone with it can empty your wallet, and there’s no way to reverse it. It is important that this private key isn’t shared at any time with anyone in your organization.
Note:
Your wallet private key is not the same as your wallet password. Once your private key is accessed, it is irreversible.
Enable two-factor authentication (2FA):
With 2FA, even if a password is stolen, a scammer would still need a second form of verification—like a code from your device or your fingerprint before logging in.
Use strong password management:
Weak or reused passwords are an open door for hackers. Use a password manager to generate strong, unique passwords and store them securely.
Beware of phishing emails and fake apps:

Phishing emails pretend to be from trusted services but send you to fake login pages while fake crypto apps may appear in app stores or be sent directly to you, designed to capture your login details and private keys. Always check the official sources before clicking links or downloading a crypto wallet.
Keep backups of your wallet:

Store your crypto assets using an offline backup wallet so you can recover your crypto if your device is damaged, lost, or hacked. With offline backups like your hardware wallet, you can securely store your crypto private keys offline, protecting them from online threats. Remember to test your backup regularly.
Conclusion

Accepting cryptocurrency is one of the easiest, fastest and borderless ways to grow your business, but it comes with the responsibility to protect your assets. Scammers are creative, fast-moving, and often hard to detect so, prevention is your best defense.
By practicing strong digital security and staying alert to suspicious activity, you can confidently accept crypto while keeping your earnings safe.
